newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS -GILTS TAKE THE HIGH ROAD ON BOE MOVE.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS -GILTS TAKE THE HIGH ROAD ON BOE MOVE.

text.p: Expectations that the Bank of England (BoE) has a firm grip on inflation and that upward pressure on interest rates is finally on the wane will put gilts on firmer ground, analysts said on Thursday.
The BoE on Thursday raised official rates by 25 basis points to 7.00 percent, but said rates had reached a level consistent with the government's inflation target.
"It's not just that people are saying, 'No more rate hikes'," said Jan Loeys, global fixed income strategist at J.P. Morgan in London.
Rather, he said, there was a perception the BoE would do what is necessary to keep inflation down.
"Now we can be confident in buying the longer end of the (gilt) curve," Loeys said.
By 1120 GMT, September gilt futures on LIFFE were 115-12, 23/32 up on the day.
Loeys said with inflation now expected to be hemmed into a range between two-to-three percent, a yield of around 7.0 percent on long gilts was attractive.
The 10-year gilt/Bund yield spread shrank to 140 basis points from 148 following the BoE move.

Economists had been expecting a rate hike, which is the fourth in as many months, but sentiment got a last minute swing after fresh evidence this week showed that the rampant consumer sector could be slowing.
Huw Roberts, European bond strategist at NatWest Markets said gilts were likely to head higher short term, but prospects for curve flattening was limited.
"I wouldn't be surprised to see it carry on in the near term because all the headlines...you'll see will be along the lines that the interest rate cycle is over for the time being," he said.
"But the curve is essentially flat already, it's difficult to know how much further that can go," added Roberts.
Economists said the BoE inflation report next week would now likely state that interest rates have reached a level consistent with the 2.5 percent inflation target.
But with bond markets seen generally under pressure from signs of a robust, and potentially inflationary, U.S. growth, gilts could see its gains capped and head lower in tandem.
"It may be that they outperform on the way down but it's still gonna be the downtrend that dominates," said Roberts. He forecast a yield of around 7.00-7.10 percent on gilts in the medium term.
He expected the gilt/Bund gap to slim to 125 basis points by the end of the year.
Mark Fox, chief European fixed income strategist at Lehman Brothers, said the rate hike had been priced in.

"The bit that came as a bit of surprise to everyone was how strong the implication of the accompanying statement was -- that that was it, no more rate rises for the time being," Fox told Reuters Financial Television.
An ensuing buying spree in gilts, particularly in the intermediate sector, was also inspired by a softer sterling rate against the mark relative to last week.

Short sterling futures are now discounting money market rates of around 7.25 percent by the end of this year, staying flat in subsequent months. The December contract stood 0.12 higher on the day at 92.67.
Earlier on Thursday a survey by the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) showed annual growth in retail sales eased slightly in July, but that high street spending was still in good shape.

The BoE has been worried about the inflationary potential of "windfall" gains totalling some 35 billion pounds which millions of Britons are receiving this year as several building societies turn themselves into banks.
